cards.q: What are top-level statements?
cards.a: Code written directly in Program.cs outside any class; the compiler wraps it in the program's Main method.

cards.q: Why is the type of Console.ReadLine() string? and not plain string?
cards.a: It returns null when there is no more input, and the ? says the string may be null.

cards.q: Which type should hold an amount of money, and why?
cards.a: decimal: it stores decimal fractions exactly, while double has rounding errors like 0.1 + 0.2.

cards.q: After int[] y = x; y[0] = 5; what is x[0]?
cards.a: 5: arrays are reference types, so x and y are the same array.

cards.q: What are 23 / 4 and 23 % 4 with ints?
cards.a: 5 and 3.

cards.q: Why is if (name != null && name.Length > 0) safe when name is null?
cards.a: && short-circuits: when the left side is false, the right side is never evaluated.

cards.q: What does $"[{x,-6}]" do?
cards.a: Writes x left-aligned in 6 characters, padded with spaces on the right.

cards.q: Why use a StringBuilder in a loop instead of +=?
cards.a: Strings are immutable, so += copies the whole string each time; StringBuilder appends in place.

cards.q: When does a do-while loop differ from a while loop?
cards.a: A do-while always runs its body at least once, because the condition is checked after the body.

cards.q: What does continue do inside a for loop?
cards.a: Skips the rest of the body for this round and goes on with the next (running the i++ part first).

cards.q: What is the difference between ref and out?
cards.a: Both pass the caller's variable; ref requires it to be assigned before the call, out requires the method to assign it.

cards.q: Can optional parameters come before required ones?
cards.a: No: optional parameters must be at the end of the list.

cards.q: Why remove items from a list inside a loop by going backwards?
cards.a: Removing shifts the later items down; going backwards means the indexes still to visit are not affected.

cards.q: After var b = a; b.Add(1); does a contain the 1?
cards.a: Yes: a and b refer to the same list.

cards.q: What happens when you read dict["missing"]?
cards.a: It throws KeyNotFoundException; use TryGetValue or GetValueOrDefault instead.

cards.q: What does HashSet.Add return for a value already in the set?
cards.a: false, and the set is unchanged.

cards.q: What is the difference between First() and FirstOrDefault()?
cards.a: First throws when nothing matches; FirstOrDefault returns the type's default (null for classes, 0 for int).

cards.q: When does a Where query actually run?
cards.a: When it is iterated, for example by foreach, ToList, Count or Sum, and again each time it is iterated.

cards.q: What does name?.Length ?? 0 give when name is null?
cards.a: 0: ?. gives null instead of throwing, and ?? replaces the null with 0.

cards.q: Why does the order of switch arms matter?
cards.a: Arms are tried from the top, and the first one that matches wins.

cards.q: What is the difference between { get; init; } and { get; set; }?
cards.a: init allows setting only while the object is created (in an initializer); set allows changing it at any time.

cards.q: Two variables hold different Point objects with the same X and Y. What does == give for a class?
cards.a: False: for classes == compares references, not contents.

cards.q: What does with do on a record?
cards.a: Creates a copy with the listed properties changed, leaving the original as it was.

cards.q: Why are mutable structs risky?
cards.a: Assignments copy them, so code often changes a copy and the original silently stays the same.

cards.q: What is the difference between abstract and virtual?
cards.a: An abstract member has no body and must be overridden; a virtual member has a default body that may be overridden.

cards.q: Can you write new Shape("x") when Shape is abstract?
cards.a: No: abstract classes cannot be instantiated, only derived from.

cards.q: How many interfaces can a class implement?
cards.a: Any number, in addition to at most one base class.

cards.q: Why does Greeter take an IClock instead of calling DateTime.Now itself?
cards.a: So a test (or another program) can give it a fixed or different clock: the behaviour can be checked and changed without editing Greeter.

cards.q: Why can a static method not use this?
cards.a: It belongs to the class, not to an object, so there is no instance for this to refer to.
cards.lessonTitle: Static Members, Extension Methods and Namespaces

cards.q: What makes a method an extension method?
cards.a: It is static, in a static class, and its first parameter is marked with this.
cards.lessonTitle: Static Members, Extension Methods and Namespaces

cards.q: What does where T : IComparable<T> allow inside a generic method?
cards.a: Calling CompareTo on values of type T, since every T is guaranteed to implement it.

cards.q: Why can a List<Circle> be passed as IEnumerable<Shape> but not as List<Shape>?
cards.a: IEnumerable<T> is read-only and covariant; a List<Shape> would allow adding other shapes into the list of circles.

cards.q: What is the type of a lambda that takes a string and returns a bool?
cards.a: Func<string, bool> (or Predicate<string>).

cards.q: Why invoke an event with TooHot?.Invoke(...)?
cards.a: If nobody subscribed, the event is null; ?. skips the call instead of throwing.

cards.q: Why should catch (Exception) come after catch (FormatException)?
cards.a: Catch blocks are tried in order; a general one first would catch everything and the specific one would never run (the compiler reports it).

cards.q: What is the difference between throw; and throw e; inside a catch?
cards.a: throw; rethrows with the original stack trace; throw e; resets the trace to the current line.

cards.q: Why is the garbage collector not enough for files?
cards.a: It frees memory at an unknown later time; a file must be closed promptly so others can use it and data is written.

cards.q: What does a using statement guarantee?
cards.a: Dispose is called when the block is left, whether normally or by an exception.

cards.q: When does the code inside an iterator method start running?
cards.a: At the first MoveNext, when the sequence is first enumerated, not when the method is called.

cards.q: Why can Fibonacci() loop forever without hanging the program?
cards.a: It is lazy: it only computes the next value when asked, and Take(10) stops asking after ten.

cards.q: What does await do to the thread while the awaited task is not finished?
cards.a: It gives the thread back to do other work; the method continues when the task completes.

cards.q: Why should you not call .Result on a task?
cards.a: It blocks the thread until the task finishes, which wastes it and can deadlock in apps with a UI thread; await instead.

cards.q: Why can count++ from several threads give a total that is too low?
cards.a: It reads, adds and writes in separate steps; two threads can read the same old value and one increment is lost.

cards.q: Who creates the CancellationTokenSource and who checks the token?
cards.a: The caller creates the source and cancels it; the worker receives the token, passes it on and checks it.

cards.q: What is the difference between File.ReadAllLines and File.ReadLines?
cards.a: ReadAllLines loads every line into an array at once; ReadLines reads lazily, one line at a time as you loop.

cards.q: Why use Path.Combine instead of joining strings with a backslash?
cards.a: The directory separator differs between operating systems; Path.Combine uses the right one and handles slashes for you.

cards.q: When can JsonSerializer.Deserialize<T> return null?
cards.a: When the JSON text is the literal null; it throws JsonException for invalid JSON instead.

cards.q: How do you make the JSON use camelCase names for PascalCase properties?
cards.a: Set PropertyNamingPolicy = JsonNamingPolicy.CamelCase in JsonSerializerOptions (or name single properties with JsonPropertyName).

cards.q: Why should one HttpClient be reused instead of creating one per request?
cards.a: Each new client can hold sockets open after use; creating many under load can exhaust them.

cards.q: Which failures are worth retrying?
cards.a: Transient ones: timeouts, 429 Too Many Requests and 5xx server errors; not 400, 401, 403 or 404.

cards.q: Why put the domain logic in a class library instead of the console project?
cards.a: So other projects (tests, a UI, a web API) can reference and reuse it, and it stays free of input/output code.

cards.q: What does dotnet run -- report 2026-03 pass to the program?
cards.a: The arguments after --: "report" and "2026-03" arrive in args.

cards.q: What is the difference between [Fact] and [Theory]?
cards.a: A Fact is one test without parameters; a Theory runs once for each set of data given with InlineData.

cards.q: Why does an InvoiceService that takes an IClock test more easily than one that reads DateTime.Now?
cards.a: A test can give it a fixed clock, so the due date is the same on every run.

cards.q: What is a composition root?
cards.a: The one place, near the program's start, where objects are created and connected; the rest of the code just receives its dependencies.

cards.q: Why should a singleton not depend on a scoped service?
cards.a: The singleton lives for the whole app and would hold on to one scoped instance forever, sharing it across all scopes.

cards.q: Why must a UI event handler not run a 5-second calculation directly?
cards.a: It runs on the UI thread, so the window freezes until it finishes; await the work (Task.Run for CPU work) instead.

cards.q: What does INotifyPropertyChanged do for data binding?
cards.a: It raises PropertyChanged when a property changes, so bound controls know to read the new value.

cards.q: Why is the report a pure function of the ledger and the month?
cards.a: It can be tested with any ledger built in memory, and it has no side effects to set up or clean up.

cards.q: Why store a version number in the saved file?
cards.a: So a later version of the app can recognise and convert files written by older versions.

cards.q: If you define `operator ==`, what else must you write?
cards.a: `operator !=`, and you should override `Equals` and `GetHashCode` so all of them agree.

cards.q: Why should an implicit conversion never throw?
cards.a: It happens without any visible code at the call site, so a failure would be a surprise nobody can see coming.

cards.q: Which collection hands out the item with the smallest priority next?
cards.a: `PriorityQueue<TElement, TPriority>`.

cards.q: What is the difference between a read-only view and an immutable collection?
cards.a: A read-only view only stops changes through that reference; the owner can still change the underlying collection. An immutable collection can never change.

cards.q: Does an attribute do anything on its own?
cards.a: No. It is metadata; something must read it (the compiler, a framework or your code) and act on it.

cards.q: Why prefer `nameof(Counter.Add)` to `"Add"` in reflection code?
cards.a: The compiler checks `nameof`, so renaming the method updates it or causes a compile error instead of a run-time failure.

cards.q: Does `numbers.AsSpan(1, 4)` copy the elements?
cards.a: No. It is a view over the same array; writing through it changes the array.

cards.q: Why can a `Span<T>` not be a field of a class?
cards.a: It may point into the stack, and a class object can outlive the method whose stack it points into.

cards.q: Why write regex patterns as `@"..."` strings?
cards.a: In a verbatim string a backslash is just a backslash, so `\d` does not have to be written `\\d`.

cards.q: Why is `ToUpper()` without a culture risky for identifiers?
cards.a: It uses the current culture, and some (Turkish, for example) change letters differently, so the same code behaves differently on different computers.

cards.q: When is an `IAsyncEnumerable<T>` better than a `Task<List<T>>`?
cards.a: When results arrive over time or there are many: the consumer can start on the first one without waiting for all of them.

cards.q: What does a bounded channel do when it is full and its mode is `Wait`?
cards.a: The writer's `WriteAsync` waits until a reader makes room: back-pressure.
